exact_claim_text: World models, learned simulators that predict how a scene evolves under action, have become the substrate on which embodied agents plan, verify and act. An agent that operates over minutes rather than seconds cannot hold every observation in its context: it must compress some observations into memory, discard others, and re-acquire the rest by looking again. Each of those three choices is a provisioning decision, and each is made today by a heuristic. Yet all three turn on a single question that has no principled answer: what must a stored observation actually preserve, and for whom?

exact_claim_text: Existing systems answer with a proxy. Latent and token compression keeps whatever minimises pixel or feature reconstruction error under a budget; episodic memory banks and retrieval-augmented world models rank records by recency or embedding similarity; KV-cache eviction keeps whatever the attention weights say was used. These methods differ in mechanism but agree in form: they reduce the quality of a memory to a single scalar, bits, or distance to the original, and therefore provision along one axis, identically for every downstream reader. When a reader underperforms, the only available response is to give it more bits.

exact_claim_text: The reason that proxy fails is not that it is coarse. It is that it measures the wrong relation. A stored record is never compared against the world; it is read. A planner extracts a symbolic predicate from it, a verifier extracts calibrated geometry, another world model extracts patch-level dynamics, and reconstruction error measures agreement with pixels, which no consumer reads. Worse, a read-out does not merely consume bits: it addresses them, under an assumed convention about what a position in the record means. Two records with identical size, identical channel rank and identical information content can therefore differ without limit in what a given reader recovers, because in one of them the information is present and unreachable. A one-dimensional byte’s axis cannot express this distinction, which is why adding bits along it can, as we measure, do nothing at all.

exact_claim_text: This tells us what to change. Memory should be provisioned on two axes, both conditioned on the consumer: how much fidelity that reader needs, and under what index the fidelity must be laid out. Staleness should be treated the same way, as a property of the reader rather than of the record, so that the choice between reading memory and looking again is decided by comparing how stale the record is to that reader against how stale a fresh look would already be by the time it arrived, rather than by comparing the two channels' costs. Improving a world model's use of memory is then not a compression problem but an interface problem: match the record's index and rank to the reader that will consume it.

exact_claim_text: We propose FRAME (Fidelity- and Reference-Aware Memory Estimation), a memory provisioning and channel-selection framework built on exactly those two axes. A memory request carries the identity of the consumer that issued it. FRAME maps that consumer to a fidelity requirement R_c(eps), the cheapest representation tier meeting the reader's error target, and to a reference-frame requirement, the index under which that tier must be laid out. It converts the record's lossiness and age into a single equivalent age A_c via a calibrated table, estimates the observation age Delta_obs a fresh look would carry given the platform's actuation profile, and selects the channel by the rule retrieve iff A_c <= Delta_obs. The rule contains no cost term, which is a measurement rather than a simplification: retrieval and re-observation never cross on compute cost over a 473,793× span of payload size. Both rule’s arguments are already known to the runtime, which tier a record is and how old it is, so nothing is estimated online; the price is paid once, offline, in calibrating the table.

exact_claim_text: We validate FRAME on CMR-Bench, a protocol we build for this purpose: 90 DAVIS and 13 SegTrack v2 videos, three real downstream consumers, seven representation tiers, nine staleness levels and three frozen backbones, with every error normalised by an age-matched zero-information floor so that 1.0 always means “this memory is worth nothing to this reader”. The central result is causal rather than correlational: holding a payload's bits exactly constant and permuting only its addressing convention costs the world-model read-out 20.7×, from 0.052 of its floors to 1.082, i.e. from near-perfect to worse than storing nothing, while costing a planner nothing measurable and a verifier 1.13×. Ablations remove every alternative explanation: giving the object-referenced family genuinely matched capacity across a 64× range moves it from 0.728 to 0.729; index and rank prove complementary, so neither substitutes for the other; the fidelity requirement inverts across consumers on the byte axis (1 byte beats 95 KB for a planner; a 1.4 KB thumbnail is worse than storing nothing for a verifier); and staleness-induced expiry is retired entirely for world models by two scalars per age, reproducing on 4 of 4 backbone×dataset sources while changing sign for the other two consumers. Assembled into the full pipeline and scored on 45 held-out videos, FRAME raises the world model's meet rate by +28.9 and +30.0 points. All 18 confirmatory claims survive Holm correction. We report no real-robot experiment, and we report in full one hypothesis we refuted and two claims we retracted.
